record.paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
record.original_question: What is the computational complexity of computing the reduced training-set-consistent subset produced by Gates' reduced nearest neighbor rule after CNN post-processing?

evidence.quote: The complexity of computing such a reduced consistent subset is an open problem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $T = \{(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{C}$ be a labeled training set, where $\mathcal{C}$ is a finite set of class labels. For a subset $S \subseteq T$, the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier $\mathrm{NN}_S : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathcal{C}$ assigns to each point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the label of the element of $S$ closest to $x$ in Euclidean distance (with ties broken by a fixed rule). The subset $S$ is said to be training-set-consistent with respect to $T$ if $\mathrm{NN}_S(x_i) = y_i$ for every $(x_i, y_i) \in T$.

Define the following two-stage reduction procedure on $T$:

1. (Condensed Nearest Neighbor, CNN) Initialize $S \subseteq T$ by Hart's procedure: start with one arbitrarily chosen element of $T$ placed in $S$, then iterate through the remaining points of $T$ (in a fixed order), adding to $S$ any point that is currently misclassified by $\mathrm{NN}_S$; repeat passes over $T$ until no more points are added.

2. (Reduced Nearest Neighbor, RNN, post-processing) Given the output $S$ of step 1, iterate through the points of $S$ (in a fixed order) and remove any point whose removal leaves a subset that is still training-set-consistent with $T$; continue until no further removal is possible. Let $S^\ast \subseteq S$ denote the resulting set.

Determine the computational complexity, as a function of $n$ and $d$, of computing $S^\ast$ from the input $T$.
artifact.status_search_result: Surveys of nearest-neighbor condensation techniques describe RNN as roughly twice as costly as CNN in practice, but no formal tight complexity bound for computing the RNN-reduced consistent subset after CNN post-processing was located in the search. The precise computational complexity appears to remain unresolved in the literature reviewed.

status_evidence.title: Survey of Nearest Neighbor Condensing Techniques
status_evidence.snippet: RNN removes instances as long as the remaining instances do not lose the property of being a consistent subset; the additional time is usually more than twice that of CNN.
status_evidence.claim: RNN is described qualitatively as costlier than CNN but no formal complexity bound is given.

status_evidence.title: The Reduced Nearest Neighbor Rule (Gates, 1972)
status_evidence.snippet: Gates' original note introduces RNN as a post-processing of CNN, removing patterns whose deletion preserves consistency.
status_evidence.claim: The original definition of the RNN rule does not establish its computational complexity.
